primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Starbucks and McDonald's said closing dine-in areas at many U.S. stores shifting to take-away and delivery. Later Starbucks would close most company-operated North America cafes for two weeks
secondary_factors: Broader market panic. Rising odds of wider lockdowns across foodservice and retail
store_description: The key stock-specific development was Starbucks move to close dine-in seating across many U.S. stores shifting business to take-away and delivery as cities tightened restrictions. The later March 20 announcement that Starbucks would close most company-operated North America cafes suggests the March 18 selloff was anticipating a much deeper traffic collapse.

primary_cause: No clear Schwab-specific negative. Fed emergency move to near-zero rates Mar 15. Rate-collapse and market-stress pressure on brokerage earnings power especially net interest revenue
secondary_factors: General financial-sector selling. Forced deleveraging
store_description: Unlike some other names Schwab does not appear to have had a fresh company-specific bombshell immediately before March 18. The more likely explanation is that investors were discounting the profit hit from the Fed emergency rate cuts toward 0% and the broader collapse in risk assets.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Simon Property said Mar 18 would temporarily close all U.S. retail properties including malls Premium Outlets and Mills until Mar 29. Total shutdown of company U.S. mall portfolio
secondary_factors: Real-estate and brick-and-mortar retail among hardest-hit segments. Rent collection risk tenant distress unknown reopening timeline
store_description: This one had an obvious issuer-specific catalyst: Simon announced it was closing all domestic retail properties an extraordinary step for the largest U.S. mall owner. A 23.7% drop makes sense because investors were suddenly pricing not just weaker tenant sales but near-immediate rent collection risk.

primary_cause: No material T-Mobile-specific negative Mar 15-18. Pending Sprint merger integration. Broad-market liquidation and de-risking
secondary_factors: Merger and integration uncertainty around Sprint likely limited defensiveness
store_description: No stock-specific negative news catalyst inside March 15-18 for T-Mobile. The drop looks more consistent with indiscriminate selling during one of the worst stretches of the COVID crash with some added sensitivity from the ongoing Sprint transaction.

primary_cause: No formal Tesla shutdown announcement in prior 3 days. Mar 18 Detroit Three shutting U.S. plants. Materially raised probability Tesla Fremont operations would be constrained
secondary_factors: General growth-stock deleveraging. Severe market-wide volatility. Repricing of auto production and distribution shutdown risk plus Tesla high-beta valuation
store_description: Tesla 16% fall was probably not driven by a single company press release but by the market rapidly internalizing that U.S. auto manufacturing was shutting down around it. Once the Detroit automakers halted plants and lockdowns expanded investors could infer heavy risk to Tesla deliveries.

primary_cause: No TXN-specific negative. Reuters described chipmakers suffering one of worst selloffs. Semiconductor-sector demand and supply fears from COVID shutdowns
secondary_factors: Industrial and auto end-market exposure especially vulnerable in mid-March 2020
store_description: TI appears to have been sold mostly as part of a semiconductor and cyclical-industrial basket rather than on a fresh company-specific event. As shutdowns spread investors reassessed demand from autos industrials and electronics.

primary_cause: Sudden collapse in mobility demand as people stopped traveling commuting and going out. No Uber-specific filing in prior 3 days but environment for ride-hailing deteriorating rapidly
secondary_factors: Profitability concerns. Funding-risk fears. General tech and high-beta deleveraging. United said Mar 16 would cut April-May capacity ~50%
store_description: The 21.6% drop fits a business model shock: cities were shutting down airport traffic was evaporating and the core ride-hailing use case was disappearing almost overnight. Even though Uber later disclosed the magnitude more explicitly the March 18 selloff was the market front-running that severe revenue damage.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in travel and cross-border payment volumes. No Visa press release in prior 3 days. Reuters later said transaction volumes deteriorated rapidly. BIS cited 19% March 2020 decline in cross-border credit card transactions at Visa
secondary_factors: Broad consumer spending fears. Market stress
store_description: Visa stock was effectively repriced for a travel shutdown. The key earnings risk was not domestic card swipes alone but the much more profitable cross-border business and later data showing cross-border volumes down 19% in March indicates the March 18 selloff was directionally correct.

primary_cause: Bank-sector stress from sudden recession shock and capital preservation moves. Large U.S. banks including Wells halted stock buybacks Mar 15
secondary_factors: Near-zero rates. Looming credit losses. General funding and market stress. Bank already carrying idiosyncratic credibility issues pre-COVID
store_description: Wells Fargo did not have a unique company-specific shock in the window but the sector did: buybacks were halted rates were slashed and investors were rapidly repricing loan losses and profitability.

primary_cause: Crude-price collapse from oil-price war plus collapsing demand. Reuters: Brent settled .36 on Mar 9 after 24.1% collapse. By Mar 18 still highlighting plunging oil prices
secondary_factors: Equity-market deleveraging. Recession fears. Energy equities being repriced for abrupt cash-flow shock
store_description: Exxon drop was not subtle or mysterious: energy equities were being repriced for an abrupt cash-flow shock as oil prices cratered and transportation demand evaporated. The combination of a Saudi-Russia supply war and a pandemic-driven demand collapse made the earnings hit immediate and severe.

primary_cause: No KO-specific press item. Restaurants stadiums theaters away-from-home venues shutting. Reuters Mar 18 emphasized broad closure of daily-life venues. Coke fountain and on-premise exposure
secondary_factors: Broad staples selling to raise cash despite defensive classification. Repricing of away-from-home beverage demand
store_description: Coke was not falling because of a discrete company announcement. It was falling because one of its highest-volume channels was disappearing as restaurants and public venues shut down. That made KO materially less defensive than the market had previously assumed.

primary_cause: No PepsiCo-specific negative. Same broad shutdown of restaurants convenience traffic entertainment venues foodservice channels
secondary_factors: Market-wide liquidation. Foodservice and out-of-home demand fears tied to shutdowns
store_description: Pepsi decline looks primarily macro-channel driven rather than news driven. Investors were reassessing the earnings mix between more resilient grocery demand and much weaker away-from-home beverage and snack demand as lockdowns broadened.

primary_cause: Sudden recession and credit-loss repricing for banks reinforced by JPM buyback halt. JPMorgan said Mar 15 would halt stock buybacks and redirect capital to lending
secondary_factors: Near-zero rates. Financial-market stress. Signaling management preference to preserve capital amid extreme uncertainty
store_description: JPMorgan had a real stock-specific item: it stopped repurchasing shares on March 15 signaling management preference to preserve capital amid extreme uncertainty. That combined with collapsing rates and fears of a deep credit cycle explains why JPM sold off harder than many non-financial blue chips.

primary_cause: No UnitedHealth-specific negative Mar 15-18. Pandemic uncertainty around medical claims testing and treatment costs and system disruption
secondary_factors: Broad-market liquidation. Market had not yet learned that deferred elective care could offset some COVID costs. Uncertainty discount rather than reaction to discrete company release
store_description: UNH move looks like an uncertainty discount rather than a reaction to a discrete company release. The market had not yet learned that deferred elective care could offset some COVID costs so investors were likely pricing a much worse immediate margin impact than ultimately materialized.

primary_cause: No negative Intuit headline. Broad growth and software selloff. Small-business stress and tax-season uncertainty during fast-moving shutdown environment
secondary_factors: Inference rather than directly reported March 15-18 company event
store_description: No stock-specific catalyst for Intuit in the 3-day window. The most likely explanation is a mix of indiscriminate selling in software and growth names and concern that shutdowns would hurt small-business customers and complicate normal tax-season behavior.

primary_cause: Market anticipation hospitals would defer elective procedures hurting robot-assisted surgery volumes. Later said COVID-driven deferral had significant negative impact. Withdrew 2020 procedure guidance
secondary_factors: General healthcare-equipment de-risking in COVID shock
store_description: March 18 was early but the market was already figuring out that hospitals would postpone non-urgent procedures to preserve capacity and reduce infection risk. Since Intuitive system usage is tightly linked to procedure volumes the stock was being repriced ahead of the company later formal guidance withdrawal.

primary_cause: Anticipation of slower consulting and project spending due to COVID. Accenture reported Mar 19 — lowered full-year revenue growth outlook because of coronavirus. Q2 revenue .1B up 7%
secondary_factors: Broad services and IT spending concerns. Mar 18 weakness likely reflected investors anticipating exactly that kind of demand slowdown
store_description: Accenture next-day results validated the concern: while the reported quarter was still solid management lowered the full-year growth outlook because of the outbreak. The March 18 decline therefore looks like the market moving ahead of an earnings-reset risk.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Reported Mar 12 record Q1 revenue .09B up 19% but said earnings included /bin/zsh.07/share hit from cancelling corporate events. Outlook missed as coronavirus affected customer spending
secondary_factors: Broad software multiple compression in the crash. Investors looking past strong reported results to COVID-related demand softness and event and customer-spending disruption
store_description: Adobe did not fall because Q1 was weak — Q1 was actually strong. The problem was that investors were repricing forward demand and enterprise spending and Adobe had already disclosed a tangible COVID hit from event cancellations which made the stock vulnerable during the March 18 risk-off wave.

primary_cause: Semiconductor-equipment sector panic over capex and supply-chain disruption. No Applied Materials-specific Mar 15-18 negative. Reuters: chipmakers suffering one of largest declines
secondary_factors: High-beta tech selling. Worsening macro conditions. Investors pricing risk that memory and foundry customers would delay tool purchases
store_description: AMAT larger-than-average drop versus TXN and AMD suggests the market was especially harsh on capex-sensitive semi-equipment names. Investors were likely pricing the risk that memory and foundry customers would delay tool purchases as the pandemic disrupted both end demand and plant operations.

primary_cause: No fresh AMD-specific negative. Reuters highlighted severe chip-stock selloff. Semiconductor-sector selloff driven by COVID supply and demand fears
secondary_factors: High-beta growth-stock deleveraging. Market reassessing everything from PC and gaming demand to supply chains and enterprise hardware spending
store_description: AMD appears to have traded more with the semiconductor complex than on issuer-specific news. In mid-March 2020 the market was reassessing everything from PC and gaming demand to supply chains and enterprise hardware spending and AMD valuation made it especially sensitive.
